title: Childhood Immunisation — SA EPI Schedule
who: Every child in South Africa; vaccines are free at public clinics
keyPoints: Birth: BCG (TB) and OPV-0 (polio, first dose)
6 weeks: hexavalent vaccine 1 (diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, polio, Hib, hepatitis B), rotavirus 1, PCV 1 (pneumonia and meningitis)
10 weeks: hexavalent 2
14 weeks: hexavalent 3, PCV 2, rotavirus 2
6 months: measles 1 (MR)
9 months: PCV 3
12 months: measles 2 (MR)
18 months: hexavalent booster
6 years: Tdap booster (at school or clinic)
12 years: Tdap booster; HPV vaccine for girls (two doses, school-based programme)
Vitamin A drops every 6 months from 6 months to 5 years, and deworming from 1 to 5 years, are given alongside

All doses are recorded in the Road-to-Health Booklet (clinic card) — keep it safe and bring it to every clinic visit; missed doses can be caught up, so never skip a visit because one was missed before

source.authority: SA NDoH Expanded Programme on Immunisation (EPI) / WHO

title: Vaccines for Adults and Older People
who: Adults, especially those with chronic conditions, pregnant women, and everyone 65 and older
keyPoints: Influenza (flu) vaccine every year before winter: free at public clinics for pregnant women, people living with HIV, chronic heart, lung and kidney conditions, diabetes, and everyone 65 and older
COVID-19 vaccination is available through the public programme — check current availability at the clinic
Pneumococcal vaccination for people 65 and older and those with chronic illness, as clinic-advised
Tetanus booster: a booster every 10 years; after a dirty or deep wound, one may be needed if the last was more than 5 years ago
Hepatitis B vaccination is offered to adults at ongoing risk, including healthcare exposure

source.authority: SA NDoH / WHO

title: HIV Testing
who: Everyone who has ever had sex — at least once a year, and with every new partner or pregnancy
keyPoints: HIV testing is free at all public clinics, and available from many pharmacies, NGOs and mobile services — with same-day results
HIV self-test kits are available free through public sector programmes — a reactive (positive) self-test is confirmed at the clinic
Testing during every pregnancy is standard, and testing the partner matters for both
Testing more often makes sense with a new partner, a known exposure, condom breakage, or symptoms of a sexually transmitted infection
Early diagnosis saves lives: treatment is one tablet a day, free, and keeps people healthy and un-infectious (undetectable equals untransmittable)
Index testing: when someone tests positive, the clinic helps their partners and children test too — with consent

source.authority: SA NDoH HIV testing services guidelines / WHO

title: TB Screening and Prevention
who: Everyone at every clinic visit; household contacts of TB patients; people living with HIV
keyPoints: Clinics screen for TB at every visit: cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss — a cough lasting more than two weeks always needs a TB test
TB tests (sputum and X-ray where needed) are free; results are usually back within days

Household contacts of a TB patient — especially children and people living with HIV — are screened and offered TB preventive therapy (TPT), a short course of medicine that stops latent TB becoming active
TPT is also standard for people living with HIV when TB is ruled out
Cough etiquette and ventilation: open windows, cough into the elbow, and let sunlight into living spaces — TB spreads in closed, crowded rooms
Finishing full TB treatment (six months) protects the household and prevents drug resistance

source.authority: SA NDoH TB guidelines / WHO

title: Cervical Cancer Screening (Pap Smear)
who: All women from age 30 (or earlier where clinically indicated); free in the public sector
keyPoints: South Africa's public sector programme offers three free Pap smears in a lifetime, at least ten years apart, from the age of 30
The test takes minutes at the clinic: cells from the cervix are checked for changes that can become cancer years later
Earlier or more frequent screening applies for women living with HIV — annually for the first three years after diagnosis, then as clinic-advised
HPV vaccination of girls at 12 (prv-001) prevents most cervical cancer in the next generation
Report between smears for: bleeding after sex, bleeding between periods, bleeding after menopause, or an unusual discharge — do not wait for the next scheduled smear
An abnormal smear usually means treating pre-cancer, not having cancer — follow-up visits matter

source.authority: SA NDoH cervical cancer screening policy / WHO

title: Breast Health Awareness
who: All women, from the teenage years onwards
keyPoints: Know what is normal for the breasts: skin, nipple direction, texture, and any lumpy areas that come and go with the monthly cycle

Changes to report at the clinic: a new lump that stays, skin dimpling like orange peel, nipple turning inward, nipple discharge or blood, one breast growing or feeling heavy, a sore that does not heal, or a lump in the armpit
Breast cancer in South Africa is often found late — knowing the signs and acting on them early saves breasts and lives
Clinical breast examination: offered at family planning and chronic visits — ask the nurse
Women with a mother or sister who had breast cancer should tell the clinic — earlier screening applies

source.authority: SA NDoH cancer control guidelines / WHO

title: Blood Pressure Checks
who: All adults at every clinic visit; at least yearly from 18, and at every antenatal visit
keyPoints: High blood pressure has no symptoms — the only way it is found is by measuring
One high reading is not a diagnosis: confirmation is several readings on different days, or home readings brought to the clinic
Public clinics check blood pressure for free at every visit — it is one of the checks that happens even when the visit is for something else
High blood pressure drives stroke, heart failure, kidney failure and blindness — it is the most important treatable silent condition in South Africa
People with diabetes, HIV, pregnancy, or a family history need more frequent checks

source.authority: SA NDoH hypertension guidelines / WHO

title: Blood Sugar (Diabetes) Screening
who: All adults at least every 3 years from 45, earlier and more often with risk factors
keyPoints: Risk factors that bring screening forward: overweight, family history of diabetes, high blood pressure, previous diabetes in pregnancy, a baby over 4kg, polycystic ovary syndrome, HIV on treatment (weight gain), and being over 35 with any of these
Screening is free at the clinic: a finger-prick sugar test, with a fasting or HbA1c test to confirm any abnormal result
Classic warning signs: passing urine often, unusual thirst, weight loss despite eating, tiredness, blurred vision, slow-healing sores
Early type 2 diabetes often has no symptoms at all for years — screening, not symptoms, finds it early
Diagnosing early protects eyes, kidneys, feet and heart before damage starts

source.authority: SA NDoH diabetes guidelines / WHO

title: Cholesterol and Heart Risk
who: Adults with risk factors: smoking, high blood pressure, diabetes, family history of early heart disease or stroke, overweight
keyPoints: Cholesterol testing is available at clinics for people with risk factors; the useful picture includes total cholesterol, LDL ('bad'), HDL ('good') and triglycerides
Heart and stroke risk builds silently from combinations: smoking, blood pressure, sugar, cholesterol, age and family history
Lifestyle changes move every one of these numbers: stopping smoking is the single biggest one, followed by daily movement, salt reduction, and losing even a little weight
People living with HIV on treatment also have heart-risk monitoring built into care over time

source.authority: SA NDoH / WHO cardiovascular risk guidance

title: Prostate Awareness for Men
who: Men from 50, or from 40-45 with a father or brother who had prostate cancer
keyPoints: Prostate cancer is among the most common cancers in South African men — and often curable when found early
Discuss prostate checking with the clinic from 50 (or 40-45 with a family history)
Warning signs to report without delay: weak or slow urine stream, straining to pass urine, blood in urine or semen, difficulty starting, or bone pain in the lower back and hips
Screening involves a blood test (PSA) and sometimes a prostate examination — the clinic will explain and obtain consent before any examination

source.authority: SA NDoH cancer control guidelines / urological societies

title: PrEP — Medicine That Prevents HIV
who: Anyone at ongoing risk of HIV — including people with HIV-positive partners, sex workers, young women in high-prevalence areas, men who have sex with men, and people who inject drugs
keyPoints: PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis) is medicine HIV-negative people take to prevent HIV — free at public clinics in South Africa
The oral form is a daily tablet; an injection given every two months is being introduced through programmes
PrEP works when taken as prescribed — the tablet needs about a week of daily dosing before it protects, and must be continued while risk continues
PrEP does not prevent pregnancy or other sexually transmitted infections — condoms still matter
Starting PrEP includes an HIV test and kidney check, with follow-up visits every few months

source.authority: SA NDoH PrEP guidelines / WHO

title: Condoms and Safer Sex
who: Everyone who is sexually active
keyPoints: Male and female condoms are free at clinics, and distributed by many NGOs, workplaces and pharmacies
Condoms prevent HIV, most sexually transmitted infections, and pregnancy — the only method that does all three
Use a new condom every time, from start to finish; check the expiry date, open the packet carefully (no teeth), pinch the tip to leave space, and use water-based lubricant only
Oil, petroleum jelly and body lotion destroy latex — never use them as lubricant
Symptoms of infection — discharge, sores, burning when passing urine — mean both partners need treatment; clinics treat STIs free and confidentially
Male and female condoms give the same protection; the female condom can be inserted up to 8 hours before sex

source.authority: SA NDoH HIV prevention guidelines / WHO

title: Medical Male Circumcision (MMC)
who: HIV-negative men and boys (from 15) choosing circumcision
keyPoints: Medical male circumcision reduces a man's risk of acquiring HIV from a female partner by about 60 percent — one of the strongest tools in the combination prevention package
MMC is free at public facilities and trained private providers in South Africa; the procedure takes about 20-30 minutes under local anaesthetic
Healing takes about 6 weeks — no sex during healing; stitches absorb on their own
MMC reduces risk; it does not remove it — condoms remain essential
Circumcision also reduces urinary infections in baby boys, and lowers the risk of penile cancer and some HPV transmission
Choose medical circumcision over traditional-only where the full procedure may not be completed — the health benefit comes from complete removal of the foreskin

source.authority: SA NDoH MMC programme / WHO

title: Handwashing
who: Everyone, every day
keyPoints: Wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds: after the toilet, before preparing or eating food, after changing nappies, after coughing or sneezing, after touching animals, and whenever hands are visibly dirty
Soap and running water is best; alcohol hand-rub (60 percent or more alcohol) works when water is not available — but not when hands are visibly dirty
Handwashing prevents diarrhoea, pneumonia, skin and eye infections, and slows outbreaks from flu to cholera — it is the single cheapest health intervention there is
Teach children the technique: wet, soap, scrub all surfaces including between fingers and thumbs and nails, rinse, dry with a clean cloth or air
No soap? Ash from a clean fire works as a rubbing agent where nothing else is available

source.authority: WHO hand hygiene guidance / SA NDoH

title: Safe Water and Household Sanitation
who: Every household, especially where water comes from tanks, rivers, boreholes or standpipes
keyPoints: Make water safe: boil it at a rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes at high altitude), or treat it with household bleach — add 1 teaspoon (5ml) of unscented household bleach (containing 5 percent chlorine) to 20-25 litres of water, mix, and wait at least 30 minutes before drinking
Store water in a clean, covered container with a tap or ladle used only for water — dipping hands and cups contaminates it
Wash the container and lid regularly with soap
Keep toilets and latrines clean and safe; never defecate in the open or near water sources
Wash hands with soap after the toilet and before food (prv-014) — safe water plus clean hands is the backbone of preventing diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid and hepatitis A
Paraffin, pesticides and bleach are stored away from water and food and never in drink bottles — accidental swallowing is a childhood emergency (Poisons Helpline 0861 555 777)

source.authority: WHO household water treatment guidance / SA NDoH environmental health

title: Malaria Prevention
who: Anyone living in or travelling to malaria areas of South Africa (mainly lowveld areas of Limpopo, Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal) and neighbouring countries, especially September to May
keyPoints: Prevent mosquito bites: sleep under an insecticide-treated net every night; cover arms and legs after dusk; use repellent (DEET-containing) on skin and clothes; use screens and close windows at night
Prophylaxis (preventive medicine) is available for travellers to high-risk areas, especially in the rainy season — start before travel, take it exactly as prescribed, and continue after returning
Season matters: risk is highest from September to May
Any fever within weeks of visiting a malaria area is malaria until proven otherwise — get tested the same day; untreated malaria can kill within 48 hours
Pregnant women and small children are at highest risk of severe malaria and need special protection and early care

source.authority: SA NDoH malaria guidelines / WHO

title: Healthy Eating and Salt Reduction
who: Everyone, at every age
keyPoints: Build meals on the healthy plate: half vegetables, a quarter starch (maize, brown bread, rice, potato), a quarter protein (beans, lentils, eggs, tinned fish, chicken, milk) — water instead of sweet drinks

Salt: keep to less than one level teaspoon (5g) a day in total, including salt already in foods — South Africa's salt legislation already lowered the salt in bread and processed foods, but stock cubes, soup powders, processed meat, crisps and instant noodles still carry most of the load
Sugar: sweet drinks (including fruit juice and energy drinks) are the biggest weight and diabetes driver — water and unsweetened amasi or milk are the everyday drinks
Fried takeaways and processed meat are for rare occasions, not weekly routine
Breastfeed babies exclusively for six months; family food for toddlers follows the same healthy plate with no added salt
Grow and buy what is in season: spinach, cabbage, carrots, butternut, beans and lentils are the affordable backbone of healthy eating

source.authority: SA food-based dietary guidelines / WHO / SA salt legislation

title: Physical Activity
who: Everyone — children, adults, older people, and people living with chronic conditions
keyPoints: Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity a week — 30 minutes on 5 days — brisk walking counts fully
Plus muscle-strengthening twice a week: carrying water, digging in the garden, or bodyweight exercises at home
Children need at least 60 minutes of active play every day
Movement lowers blood pressure, controls sugar and weight, lifts mood, strengthens bones and prevents falls in older age — it is medicine without a prescription
Start where you are: ten-minute walks build to thirty; taking stairs, walking to the shop, and getting off a taxi rank early all count
Anyone with a heart condition, chest pain or long-standing diabetes should check in at the clinic before starting hard exercise — walking is safe for almost everyone

source.authority: WHO physical activity guidelines

title: Stopping Smoking
who: Every person who smokes or uses snuff, hubbly or e-cigarettes
keyPoints: Quitting is the single most powerful health change a smoker can make — heart and stroke risk starts falling within weeks, and lung cancer risk halves after ten smoke-free years
Smoking harms more than the smoker: children in smoking households get more pneumonia, asthma attacks and ear infections
Nicotine replacement (patches, gum, lozenges) roughly doubles quit success — ask at the clinic or pharmacy
Practical quitting: set a quit date, tell people, remove cigarettes, lighters and ashtrays, plan for the three hardest trigger moments of the day, and expect cravings to pass within five minutes
Hubbly (hookah) is not safe — one session can deliver the smoke of many cigarettes; e-cigarettes also carry dependence and harm
Free quit support is available — clinics, SADAG, the National Council Against Smoking and CANSA all offer programmes and advice lines

source.authority: WHO / CANSA / National Council Against Smoking

title: Alcohol — Cutting the Risk
who: Everyone who drinks alcohol
keyPoints: No level of drinking improves health — the safest amount for health is none, and any reduction helps
Harmful patterns to change: drinking more than planned, drinking to cope, binge sessions (four or more drinks in one sitting for women, five for men), and drinking around children's needs or work
No alcohol at all during pregnancy or while breastfeeding — South Africa has among the highest rates of fetal alcohol spectrum disorder in the world, and there is no safe amount
Never drink and drive, ride a motorbike, or supervise water activities — alcohol is a factor in many road deaths and drownings
Alcohol interacts dangerously with many medicines: sleeping tablets, pain tablets, epilepsy and TB treatment — ask the clinic about the specific medicine
Worried about your own or someone else's drinking? Help is free — see the substance-use entry (mh-006) for SANCA and helpline options

source.authority: WHO / SA NDoH / SANCA
